description: Hey, everyone! We're IGNIS5, a team of curious minds excited to explore space science through our challenge, Flame in Freefall! We love creativity, brainstorming, and turning interesting ideas into something amazing.
summary: Our project, Flame in Space focuses on fire safety in space. Fire in space is more different than in Earth because of oxygen and microgravity level. It makes predict fire during space missions. For solving this issue we developed a website that helps users understand the risk of fire in space. People can enter different environmental parameters such as oxygen concentration, gravity, airflow ,and our website will analyze these inputs to calculate the risk. Our website helps people understand how different conditions can affect fire risks. It can also support fire safety in space.
details:
Our project includes three main features.

First, the Mission Matcher enables users to select environments such as the International Space Station, a lunar space base, or a spacesuit. The dashboard then ranks six NASA experiments according to how closely their conditions match the selected environment. It also provides a comparison of the fuels, oxygen levels, and airflow speeds used in those experiments.

Second, the Flame Risk Predictor allows users to adjust oxygen concentration, airflow speed, and gravity using interactive sliders based on findings from NASA's BASS and FLEX investigations. It provides an indication of possible flame behavior, including whether a flame may extinguish, spread, or develop into cool-flame combustion. It also takes smoke behavior and fire detection into account.

Third, the AI Interpreter and Experiment Generator analyzes the selected conditions, produces a short scientific explanation, identifies relevant graphs from existing research, and suggests possible future experiments.

Our project, IGNIS5, is invaluable to a wide range of users, from ordinary students to professional engineers, space explorers, and researchers.

Our project specifically focuses on two essential research challenges that often cause confusion.

First, the oxygen challenge. Lunar habitats may use oxygen concentrations of approximately 30–34%, which raises additional fire safety concerns.

Second, the lack of gravity-related experimental data. There is significantly less experimental fire data under lunar gravity (1/6 g) and Martian gravity (3/8 g) than under Earth's gravity or microgravity conditions.

IGNIS5 aims to highlight these research gaps and indicate where additional experiments are needed.

We expect our project to help people interested in this field understand flame behavior in various space environments in a clear and accessible way.

It will also help users explore complex scientific concepts through simple explanations and illustrations, making the material easier to understand.

We hope that our program will be useful not only to students but also to professional researchers, engineers, and other specialists.

Ultimately, it will bring us one step closer to uncovering the mysteries of the boundless ocean of space.

We used *Lovable*, an AI-powered platform, to develop our interactive web application. We provided our own text, project ideas, instructions, and feature descriptions to build the three main functions: Mission Matcher & Ranker, Risk & Flame Predictor, and AI Interpreter & Experiment Generator.

For scientific research and reliable information, we used official NASA resources, including NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), and research materials about the BASS, SAFFIRE, SAME, FLEX, CFI-G, and E-FIELD experiments.

We use special scenarios to spark people's curiosity and make them feel like heroes or winners because they get to make important decisions. For example, they can choose oxygen concentrations and other gases to create safe conditions for human life beyond Earth.

This interactive approach attracts people's attention and helps them retain information for longer.

We also take into account the fact that fire is one of the most dangerous hazards in our lives. However, in space, flames may behave unpredictably, potentially putting astronauts at risk due to their vulnerability in such extreme environments.

We truly appreciate astronauts for their bravery and for the valuable scientific data they provide us with.

Therefore, we believe that our first priority must be ensuring the safety of astronauts and scientific equipment. This would lead to better research outcomes and pave the way for new, more valuable discoveries.
